narrative: A docs-only design PR (charter, design, two research docs) went through five full review rounds and 110 findings before hitting the round cap. The reviewer was almost always right and the agent accepted nearly everything. The one wrong call was F42, where the agent argued charter compliance inside design.md instead of amending the charter; F65 caught it. 61 of 110 findings came from earlier fixes. Three patterns account for most of them: fixes that swept only the lines the reviewer named (citations, verb coverage, research-doc design language); fixes whose new text contradicted another section or added a new overclaim; and new security mechanisms (majority threshold, succession, replay attestation, re-enrollment) with holes in their own authorization. Every round also surfaced pre-existing issues (for example F67, F93, F104), so no round was avoidable outright. The fix-caused share grew each round.
guidance_observations: Each fix commit answered threads one by one. A single 'grep every restatement of what I just changed' pass before pushing would have prevented most comment_drift and same_gap findings.
Twice (F72, F109) a 'Fixed in <sha>' reply described a change the commit did not contain; reading the diff before replying would have caught both.

New authorization mechanisms added as fixes (owner majority, succession, re-enrollment, replay version) were never checked against the adversary model the doc already states, so each one came back as an S4 in the next round.
Synthesis claims in competitors.md were narrowed three times (F33, F64, F88/F98) without rechecking each named product against its own section, so each narrowing created a new overclaim.

For a design doc this size, a self-review against the charter's own process and the feature-surface strain points before the first push would have caught many pre-existing gaps that otherwise surfaced one per round.
